source_text: Ergo in operibus eius nullus pudor est; in sententiis autem summa deformitas. Certum est nempe, quod poenam mereatur reatus; num ideo tamen confusio culpae debita, in vindicta recurrit, ut appelletur sine pudore quod fecit reus, sed non possit sine ignominia dici quod iudicando fecit Deus?
pass_a_gloss: Therefore in his works there is no modesty; but in his sentences the highest deformity. It is certain indeed that guilt deserves penalty; yet does therefore the confusion owed to fault run back in the vengeance, so that what the guilty one did may be named without shame, but what God did by judging cannot be said without ignominy?

lemmas.lexica: LS opus; Blaise God's works vs devil's

pass_b_english: So there is no shame in his works, but the greatest ugliness in his sentences! Guilt certainly deserves punishment. But does the disgrace due to guilt therefore pass into the punishment, so that what the guilty person did can be named without shame, while what God did in judging cannot be spoken of without dishonor?

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
